paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Today, in the 21st century AD, we like to think that we are living through a period when technology has an unparalleled hold on society, but it is nothing compared with that of the ancient world, when invention and technology were the most powerful forces shaping civilization. Indeed, technology was the one factor that made all other changes - social, political and cultural - possible. The single largest step in early man's social evolution came around 8000 BC, with the invention of animal husbandry and agriculture. This enabled people to progress from living in nomadic communities to settling in small towns. The progress was brought about by a combination of climatic change and the invention of more efficient hunting tools, of a means of controlling and utilizing fire to clear undergrowth, and of ways of building lasting shelters. It led to a massive growth in population, which in turn triggered a further rapid increase in technological innovation. Most of this change took place in the eastern Mediterranean, where the climate and the annual flooding of fertile soils favoured the development of agriculture, and later brought about the growth of cities such as Babylon in present-day Iraq. By around 6500 BC, Jericho is believed to have been the largest city in the world, with a population of approximately 2,500.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: By around 2500 BC, the urban revolution had brought about a momentous cultural transition that in turn generated new needs. These were met by a giant leap in technological innovation. For the first time manufacturing became established, as man invented ways of making textiles, firing ceramics and producing metalwork. This prompted barter methods to evolve into more sophisticated trading arrangements, culminating in the invention of early money. With these technological changes came a corresponding increase in the complexity of the social and political organization of human groups, which in turn necessitated the transcription of language, first to keep track of trading arrangements, then to communicate and record events, processes, philosophies and, of course, inventions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The history of inventiori is littered with useless devices that never caught on, but the first and second millennia BC were periods of invention for the sake of necessity. And in contrast with the modern era, in which science provides the basis for technological developments, scientific knowledge was limited and technological skills were handed down through generations. However, by the time that Mediterranean city states were flowering, between approximately 800-600 BC, scientist-inventors began to emerge. Figures such as Hero, Strato, Cresibus and Philon used observations and measurements of the physical and natural world to design inventions. However, important though these men were, they were all dwarfs when compared with Archimedes, the Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, inventor and astronomer of the third century BC. Here was a man of calibre that the world would not see again for almost two thousand years.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Many misconceptions surround the development of technology during the first millennium AD. '.he popul~r i~age is that of the technical and cultural achievements of the Roman Empire collapsing in the fifth century, and being followed by a period often known as the Dark Ages, when creativity ceased. However, there was little about the period between the fifth and tenth century that was dark or backward. Following the collapse of the Roman Empire, the eastern civilizations of Islam, India and China became the new centres of technological and scientific innovation. In China, technical skills were highly valued by government officials, who prevented any new method or machine from being introduced unless it offered a clear benefit. The stability of their rule allowed paper, the lock gate, the abacus, the first mechanical clock and gunpowder to be developed. Meanwhile, India and the Islamic world built on the scientific attainments of Greece, and made significant breakthroughs in the fields of mathematics, astronomy, architecture and clock making.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In Western Europe at this time, the most profound influence was the invasion of certain countries by Teutonic and Viking tribes, who brought with them various innovations. The invaders are thought to have spread the use of stirrups, saddles and metal mouthpieces for horse riding, and made several improvements in ship design. The Teutonic tribes also improved upon the plough to turn the heavy soils of northern Europe, which were forested. By 1 OOO AD, new agricultural techniques had resulted in grain surpluses. This led many peasants to abandon small, individual farming plots in favour of the successful medieval communal pattern of open-field agriculture. As there was a big demand for barrel makers, metal workers and leather workers, others chose to pursue skilled work in towns and cities.
